judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 79, which requires cities and counties to allow apartment buildings near major transit stops on land already zoned for housing, commercial, or mixed use. Minimum height, density, and floor-area standards rise the closer a site sits to the stop. Projects must meet affordability, demolition and antidisplacement, and labor standards, and a local government may adopt its own transit-oriented plan in place of the state standards. It passed the California State Assembly 43-19 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 627, which makes it a crime, chargeable as an infraction or a misdemeanor, for a law enforcement officer to wear a face covering that conceals their identity while performing their duties. The law counts federal agents and officers of other states operating in California as law enforcement officers. Exemptions cover undercover and tactical operations, occupational health and safety law, protecting an identity during prosecution, and disability accommodations. Every agency operating in the state must post a written facial-covering policy by July 1, 2026, and officers of an agency that posts a compliant policy by that date are exempt from the criminal penalty. It passed the California State Assembly 45-23 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass AB 495, the Family Preparedness Plan Act of 2025, which widens the range of relatives who may sign a caregiver's authorization affidavit to enroll a child in school and consent to school-related medical care. A court may appoint an adult the custodial parent names as a joint guardian when that parent will be temporarily unavailable, including because of an immigration-related administrative action. Records of those guardianship proceedings are confidential. Local educational agencies must keep their immigration-enforcement policies current with the Attorney General's guidance. Licensed child care facilities are barred from collecting immigration-status information and must report law-enforcement requests for information or access to the facility. It passed the California State Senate 29-10 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 580, which requires the Attorney General to publish, by July 1, 2026, model policies for state and local agencies on interacting with immigration authorities. The Attorney General must also publish guidance and audit criteria for limiting how far the information in government databases is available for immigration enforcement. State and local agencies must adopt the model policy or an equivalent one by January 1, 2027. It passed the California State Assembly 58-19 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 704, which bars selling or transferring a firearm barrel unless the transaction is completed in person through a licensed firearms dealer. Exemptions include law enforcement agencies, the military, licensed dealers and curio collectors, estate transfers, barrels attached to a firearm, and barrels bought in the same transaction as a firearm with its own eligibility check. Possessing firearm barrels with the intent to sell them is also barred unless the seller is a licensed dealer. From July 1, 2027 the dealer must run an eligibility check on the buyer, for a fee of up to $5, and record the transaction. A first or second violation is a misdemeanor, and further violations may be charged as felonies. It passed the California State Assembly 57-20 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass AB 325, which lets an antitrust complaint under California's Cartwright Act proceed when it pleads facts showing a conspiracy to restrain trade is plausible. Such a complaint need not allege facts tending to rule out independent action. The law also makes it unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of such a conspiracy, or to coerce another business into adopting the price or term the algorithm recommends. It passed the California State Senate 29-9 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass AB 692, which makes it unlawful to require a worker, in an employment contract entered into on or after January 1, 2026, to accept stay-or-pay terms. Stay-or-pay terms make a worker owe an employer, training provider, or debt collector money if the worker's job ends. Exceptions include government loan-repayment programs, qualifying tuition contracts for transferable credentials, approved apprenticeships, qualifying discretionary signing bonuses, and residential-property contracts. The banned terms are declared void as restraints on a lawful trade. A worker subjected to them may sue, on their own behalf or for others in the same position, for civil penalties and other relief. It passed the California State Senate 25-11 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass AB 1415, which extends the Office of Health Care Affordability's oversight to management services organizations and adds definitions for investor owners such as hedge funds. Management services organizations must submit data to the office. Mergers and other transactions involving those organizations, or the entities that own or control them, require advance written notice to the office. It passed the California State Senate 26-10 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass AB 1319, which makes it unlawful in California to import, export, transport, sell, buy, or possess for sale any fish, wildlife, or plant taken in violation of a wildlife law. The ban covers violations of state and federal wildlife laws as those laws stood on January 19, 2025, and seized evidence is forfeited on conviction. The law also requires the Department of Fish and Wildlife to publish findings adding a species to a provisional candidate list when federal protections for it are reduced. These provisions expire at the end of 2031. It passed the California State Senate 25-10 and became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to pass SB 42, the California Fair Elections Act of 2026, which repeals the state ban on public campaign financing for candidates who accept spending limits and meet qualifying criteria. Public funds may not be spent on legal defense or on repaying a candidate's own loans to their campaign, and the fine for contributions by foreign governments rises. Because it amends the voter-approved Political Reform Act, its provisions take effect only if voters approve them at the November 3, 2026 statewide general election. It passed the California State Assembly 59-20 and became law.
